text:
Round one. Ten thousand euros into world stocks on the last day of 1999. Right at the top.

Dividends reinvested, measured in euros, after a zero point two percent yearly fee. No cherry picking.

By the end of 2002, your ten thousand euros had become five thousand five hundred.

Forty-five percent gone in three years. And this is the whole world index, not a tech fund.

Then the recovery. By the end of 2006 you're at eight thousand seven hundred. Almost there.

And then, 2008. By the end of that year, your portfolio is worth five thousand three hundred euros.

Nine years in, you have less money than at the bottom of the dot-com crash.

You're only back above ten thousand euros in 2013. Thirteen years of doing everything right, and nothing to show for it.

Start investing at thirty-five, and you'd be close to fifty before you saw a profit.

And that's before inflation. With prices rising around two percent a year, your money only got its purchasing power back in 2015. Sixteen years.

Start one year later, in January 2001, and it took twelve years, which is what I showed in one of my Shorts. Start at the end of 2006, just before the financial crisis, and it took six.

And it wasn't a quiet thirteen years. The largest year-end drop on the way was almost forty-seven percent.

Now the other side. That same ten thousand euros, invested at the worst possible moment, is worth about forty-six thousand euros today.

That's about five point nine percent a year for almost twenty-seven years. After the dot-com crash, 2008, Covid and 2022.

Prices in the euro area rose about seventy-six percent from 1999 to 2025. So in today's money, you still ended with about two and a half times what you put in.

So buying at the top did not ruin you. Selling at the bottom would have. We'll come back to that.

But one start date is just one story. So I ran every start year from 2000 to 2016, and every holding period from one to ten years.

Each cell is the total return of a lump sum. Green made money. Red lost money.

Out of one hundred and seventy combinations, forty-five lost money. More than one in four.

Almost all of the red sits in two places: if you started between 2000 and 2002, or right before 2008.

Look at the last column, ten years. Seventeen ten-year windows, and three of them still lost money.

The worst one: start at the end of 1999, and ten years later you're down thirty-three percent.

The best one: start at the end of 2011, and ten years later you're up two hundred and sixty-seven percent.

Same index, same fund, same discipline. The only difference was the year you started.

Now turn the table into one number per holding period: how often did you lose money?

Up to five years, roughly a third of the time. From seven years on, about one in six. In this data, the odds only really improved after six or seven years.

A caveat: that's only seventeen start years, and they include two of the worst crashes in a century. Longer histories look better. But this is the history Europeans with euro ETFs actually lived.

And notice this: in this data, nobody who started near a bubble peak was saved by waiting five years. The only thing that reliably fixed it was time, and new money.
